Foods spelled with a double letter.Broccoli: The double C is Italian, where the name means little sprouts; broccoli is a cultivated cabbage relative bred from wild mustard-family plants.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Zucchini: The double C in this Italian word, and the squash, is the plural of zucchino; the flowers are a delicacy too, often stuffed and fried.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Coffee: Double F and double E: it is one of the few common words with two double letters; legend says an Ethiopian goat herder spotted its energy.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Apple: The double P is in a fruit with about 7,500 varieties worldwide, and a typical apple floats because about a quarter of its volume is air.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Cheese: The double E is in a food made in thousands of varieties; there is evidence of cheese-making in pottery from about 7,000 years ago.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Spaghetti: Both double G and double T appear in it; in Italian it means little strings, and the plural is what we eat, as spaghetto is rarely used.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Pepper: The double P is in a spice once so valuable it was used to pay rent and taxes, nicknamed black gold in medieval Europe.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Cookie: The double O is from the Dutch koekje, little cake, and the word came to America with Dutch settlers in New Amsterdam.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Muffin: The double F is in a treat; England's old muffin is a flat yeast bread, and the sweet cupcake-shaped version is American.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Butter: The double T is in butter, made by churning cream until fat clumps separate from buttermilk, a process known for thousands of years.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Carrot: The double R is in a vegetable that was originally purple or yellow; orange carrots were popularized in the Netherlands in the 1600s.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Pizza: Double Z: the word first appears in a document from Gaeta, Italy, in the year 997, long before tomatoes arrived in Europe.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Waffle: The double F appears in waffle, a word from Dutch wafel, and in Belgium the batter is yeast-raised, making a lighter, crisper result.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Banana: A trap: it has three As and two Ns, but none are doubled; bananas are technically berries, while strawberries are not.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Tomato: No double letter, a trap for people expecting one; the tomato is botanically a fruit, and the US Supreme Court ruled it a vegetable for tariffs in 1893.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Potato: No double letters in it; it was the first vegetable grown in space, in 1995, aboard the space shuttle Columbia.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Lemon: None of its letters repeat in a row; lemons are likely a hybrid of citron and bitter orange, and sailors used them against scurvy.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Bacon: No double letters here; bacon is so beloved that it had a name in Old English, and the idiom bring home the bacon is centuries old.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Onion: No double letter in onion, though its layers may make you think otherwise; the sulfur compound that makes eyes tear is released when cells are cut.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Mango: No doubled letters; the mango is the national fruit of India, Pakistan and the Philippines, and is related to cashews and poison ivy.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Taco: Taco has no double letter; it likely began as a Mexican silver-mining term for a small charge wrapped in paper.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Celery: No doubled letter, a trap with the many Es; celery is mostly water, about 95 percent, and was used as medicine before it was food.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Garlic: No double letters in garlic; a clove has been found in Egyptian tombs, and ancient builders of the pyramids reportedly ate it for strength.
Foods spelled with a double letter.Bagel: No doubled letters; the bagel is boiled before baking, which gives it a chewy crust, and it is said to date to 1610 Kraków.

Countries that use the euro.France: French euro coins carry the national motto Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité, and the first euro coins appeared in 2002.
Countries that use the euro.Italy: Italy's 1 euro coin shows Leonardo's Vitruvian Man, and its 2 euro coin shows the poet Dante.
Countries that use the euro.Spain: Spain's 10, 20 and 50 cent coins show Cervantes, author of Don Quixote.
Countries that use the euro.Portugal: Portugal's euro coins show royal seals and castles, and it was one of the first 11 countries to adopt the euro.
Countries that use the euro.Netherlands: Dutch coins showed Queen Beatrix, then King Willem-Alexander from 2014.
Countries that use the euro.Belgium: Brussels hosts the European Commission and Council, yet Belgian coins show its king.
Countries that use the euro.Austria: Austria's 1 euro coin features Mozart, and Vienna is the seat of OPEC.
Countries that use the euro.Ireland: Irish euro coins show the harp, the national emblem, which also appears on Guinness labels.
Countries that use the euro.Finland: Finland's 1 euro coin shows two flying swans, and its 2 euro coin features cloudberries.
Countries that use the euro.Greece: Greece joined in 2001 and its coins show owls, ancient Athens's emblem.
Countries that use the euro.Estonia: Estonia joined the euro in 2011, and its coins show the country's outline.
Countries that use the euro.Croatia: Croatia adopted the euro on 1 January 2023, replacing the kuna, whose name means marten, the animal.
Countries that use the euro.Slovakia: Slovakia joined in 2009 and its coins show the Bratislava Castle and a double cross.
Countries that use the euro.UK: A trap. The UK keeps the pound sterling, one of the oldest currencies still in use.
Countries that use the euro.Switzerland: Switzerland is neither in the EU nor the eurozone, and it uses the Swiss franc.
Countries that use the euro.Sweden: In the EU, but Swedes rejected the euro in a 2003 referendum and kept the krona.
Countries that use the euro.Denmark: Denmark has an opt-out from the euro, but the krone is tied closely to the euro's value.
Countries that use the euro.Norway: Outside the EU, Norway keeps the krone, while its oil fund, the world's largest sovereign fund, holds shares in thousands of companies.
Countries that use the euro.Poland: An EU member that kept its zloty, which means golden.
Countries that use the euro.Czech Republic: The Czechs kept the koruna, Czech for crown, though they are in the EU.
Countries that use the euro.Hungary: Hungary uses the forint, named after Florence's gold florin, despite EU membership.
Countries that use the euro.Iceland: Iceland has its own króna and is outside the EU. The króna collapsed in the 2008 crisis.
Countries that use the euro.Romania: Romania is in the EU, but still uses the leu, which means lion.

Lakes of North America.Superior: It is the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area, and it holds about 10 percent of the world's fresh surface water.
Lakes of North America.Michigan: The only Great Lake entirely within the United States, and linked to Lake Huron, it is technically one lake with it.
Lakes of North America.Huron: It has the longest shoreline of any Great Lake, thanks to thousands of islands, including Manitoulin, the biggest lake island in the world.
Lakes of North America.Erie: The shallowest and warmest of the Great Lakes, it freezes over most often in winter.
Lakes of North America.Ontario: The smallest Great Lake by area, fed by the Niagara River after the famous falls.
Lakes of North America.Tahoe: Straddling California and Nevada, this Sierra Nevada lake is about 500 m deep and clear enough to see far down.
Lakes of North America.Great Salt Lake: Utah's lake is saltier than the ocean, and in recent years it has been shrinking.
Lakes of North America.Great Bear Lake: It is the largest lake entirely within Canada, lying in the Northwest Territories above the Arctic Circle.
Lakes of North America.Lake Winnipeg: This Manitoba lake is one of the largest in Canada, and it drains north to Hudson Bay.
Lakes of North America.Lake Champlain: Between Vermont, New York and Quebec, it supposedly has its own monster, Champ.
Lakes of North America.Crater Lake: Oregon's lake fills a collapsed volcano, and at about 594 m it is the deepest lake in the United States.
Lakes of North America.Lake Okeechobee: Florida's largest lake is shallow and feeds the Everglades.
Lakes of North America.Lake Louise: In Banff National Park, Alberta, its turquoise color comes from fine rock flour from glaciers.
Lakes of North America.Baikal: Siberia's Lake Baikal is the deepest on Earth, over 1,600 m, so it belongs to Russia and not North America.
Lakes of North America.Titicaca: On the border of Peru and Bolivia, it is the highest large lake that ships can navigate.
Lakes of North America.Victoria: Africa's biggest lake feeds the White Nile, and it lies in East Africa, far from North America.
Lakes of North America.Loch Ness: Scotland's long, deep lake is famed for its monster legend, and it is not in North America.
Lakes of North America.Como: Italy's Y-shaped lake, over 400 m deep, has long been a retreat for celebrities, and it is in Europe.
Lakes of North America.Garda: Italy's largest lake lies at the foot of the Alps, and is a European, not North American, lake.
Lakes of North America.Balaton: Hungary's shallow lake is the largest in Central Europe, so it belongs to Europe, not North America.
Lakes of North America.Ladoga: Europe's largest lake lies in northwest Russia, near St Petersburg.
Lakes of North America.Tanganyika: This African lake is the world's longest freshwater lake, stretching about 670 km.
Lakes of North America.Malawi: This East African lake is famed for hundreds of colorful cichlid fish species.
Lakes of North America.Lake Eyre: Australia's Lake Eyre, a vast salt pan that is usually dry, fills only after rare floods and then draws huge flocks of birds.

Former names of countries.Ceylon: The island's name until 1972, when it became Sri Lanka. It still names the famous tea, and Ceylon cinnamon is considered the true cinnamon.
Former names of countries.Siam: Thailand's name until 1939 (and briefly again in 1945 to 1949). It gave English Siamese cats and Siamese twins, after Chang and Eng Bunker, born there.
Former names of countries.Persia: The Western name for Iran until 1935, when the government asked the world to use Iran. Persian carpets and Persian cats keep the old name alive.
Former names of countries.Rhodesia: Named for Cecil Rhodes, this British colony declared independence in 1965 under white minority rule and became Zimbabwe in 1980.
Former names of countries.Zaire: The country's name from 1971 to 1997 under Mobutu Sese Seko, before it turned back into the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Former names of countries.Abyssinia: The old European name for Ethiopia, from a word for the highland peoples. It was one of the few African states never colonized, apart from a brief Italian rule.
Former names of countries.Dahomey: The West African kingdom was famed for its all-female Agojie warriors. The republic renamed itself Benin in 1975, taking a name from a different old kingdom.
Former names of countries.Upper Volta: The country was named for the Volta river's upper reaches, then renamed Burkina Faso in 1984 by Thomas Sankara. The new name means land of upright people.
Former names of countries.Kampuchea: The Khmer name for Cambodia, used officially under Khmer Rouge rule from 1975 and the People's Republic of Kampuchea until 1989.
Former names of countries.Swaziland: King Mswati III renamed it Eswatini in 2018, the 50th anniversary of independence, saying he wanted to drop the colonial name. It means land of the Swazis.
Former names of countries.Burma: Myanmar's ruling junta changed the English name in 1989. Some countries and people still use Burma, which is why both are heard today.
Former names of countries.Sri Lanka: This is the current name, adopted in 1972, so it's not a former one. It was named Ceylon before that, and the island is famous for its tea.
Former names of countries.Thailand: The present name, which means land of the free. It's not a former name, but Siam was the name it was known by earlier.
Former names of countries.Iran: The current name, which locals have always used themselves. Persia was the name the outside world used, so Iran isn't a former name.
Former names of countries.Myanmar: This is the current official name since 1989, so it's not a former one. The older name Burma remains in wide use abroad.
Former names of countries.Zimbabwe: The name comes from the stone ruins of Great Zimbabwe and means stone houses. It's the current name, replacing Rhodesia in 1980.
Former names of countries.Ethiopia: Today's name, long used by Ethiopians. Abyssinia was the former outsider's term, so Ethiopia itself is not a former name.
Former names of countries.Benin: The current name since 1975, so not a former one. Benin was a separate old kingdom famous for its bronze plaques, and Dahomey was its former name.
Former names of countries.Burkina Faso: This is the present name, adopted in 1984, so it replaced Upper Volta. It means land of upright people, joining words from two local languages.
Former names of countries.Cambodia: The present name, so not a former one, though it briefly went by Kampuchea. It's home to Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument on Earth.
Former names of countries.Eswatini: The current name since 2018, so it's not a former one. It replaced Swaziland, and it's one of the last absolute monarchies in the world.
Former names of countries.Bangladesh: It became independent from Pakistan in 1971, but this was not a former name of a country. Before that it was East Pakistan, a province.
Former names of countries.Namibia: Named after the Namib desert, this has been the name since independence in 1990. Before that it was South West Africa, a territory, not a country.
Former names of countries.Tanzania: Not a former name. It was created in 1964 by merging Tanganyika and Zanzibar, with the name blending the two.

Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Talc: Number 1 on the Mohs scale, so soft a fingernail scratches it. Ground to powder, it becomes the baby powder in many bathrooms.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Gypsum: Number 2, soft enough to scratch with a fingernail. It's the main ingredient in drywall, plaster of Paris and chalkboard-style classroom chalk.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Calcite: Number 3, the main mineral in limestone and marble. Clear crystals of it split light into a double image.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Fluorite: Number 4. It can glow under ultraviolet light, a phenomenon named fluorescence after this mineral.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Apatite: Number 5. Its name comes from the Greek for deceive, since it was often mistaken for other minerals. Your teeth and bones contain a form of it.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Orthoclase: Number 6, a feldspar. Its name means break straight, because it cleaves at right angles. Feldspars are the most common minerals in Earth's crust.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Quartz: Number 7, one of the most common minerals in Earth's crust. Quartz crystals vibrate at precise rates, which is why they keep watches ticking accurately.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Topaz: Number 8. It is hard enough to scratch quartz and was a standard of the scale from the start.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Corundum: Number 9, the mineral that forms rubies and sapphires. Its grit is also used industrially as an abrasive.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Diamond: Number 10, the hardest natural material, scratched only by another diamond. On an absolute scale it is far harder than corundum, not just one step up.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Granite: A trap: it is a rock made from several minerals, not a single mineral with a Mohs number. Its quartz is hard, its mica soft.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Marble: A trap: a rock made of calcite crystals, not a mineral itself. Calcite sits at 3 on the Mohs scale, the reason marble scratches easily.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Emerald: A trap: emerald is a gem variety of beryl, which rates 7.5 to 8. It isn't one of the ten reference minerals.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Jade: A trap: jade is a gemstone, either jadeite or nephrite, not a reference mineral. It's tough rather than especially hard.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Amber: A trap: it's fossilized tree resin, not a mineral, and is soft enough, about 2 to 2.5 on Mohs, to be cut with a knife.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Obsidian: A trap: it's a volcanic glass with no crystal structure, so it is not a mineral at all, and not on the scale.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Graphite: A trap: it's a real mineral, but it's not a reference point. It's very soft, about 1 to 2, so it leaves marks on paper.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Mica: A trap: a real mineral that peels into sheets, but not a reference point. It's about 2 to 3.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Pyrite: A trap: fool's gold is a real mineral, hard at 6 to 6.5, but it isn't a reference point on the scale.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Halite: A trap: rock salt is a mineral rated about 2.5, yet it is not one of the ten reference minerals.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Opal: A trap: opal is a gemstone with no crystal structure at all, rated about 5.5 to 6.5, and not a reference mineral.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Gold: A trap: gold is soft, about 2.5 to 3, which is why jewelry gold is alloyed with other metals. It's not a reference point.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Coal: A trap: coal is a rock made of plant remains, not a mineral, and has no Mohs number as a reference.
Minerals on the Mohs hardness scale.Pearl: A trap: built by oysters in layers of calcium carbonate, it's organic, soft at about 2.5 to 4.5, and not a mineral on the scale.

Diseases caused by bacteria.Tuberculosis: Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, it still kills over a million people a year. Its waxy cell wall makes the bacteria slow to treat.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Strep throat: Caused by Streptococcus pyogenes. Untreated, it can lead to rheumatic fever, which is why doctors prescribe antibiotics for it.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Cholera: In 1854 John Snow traced a London outbreak to one water pump, helping found modern epidemiology. The bacterium spreads through contaminated water.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Tetanus: Caused by Clostridium tetani spores living in soil. It isn't passed person to person, and a booster shot every ten years protects against it.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Lyme disease: Named for Lyme, Connecticut, where it was recognized in the 1970s. The Borrelia bacteria are spread by the bite of tiny blacklegged ticks.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Whooping cough: Also called pertussis, it gets its name from the gasping 'whoop' after a coughing fit. A bacterium, Bordetella pertussis, causes it.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Typhoid: Caused by Salmonella Typhi. 'Typhoid Mary' Mallon, a cook in early 1900s New York, spread it while showing no symptoms herself.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Botulism: The toxin from Clostridium botulinum is among the most poisonous substances known. In tiny doses, it is the basis of Botox.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Leprosy: Also called Hansen's disease after the doctor who found its bacterium in 1873. It is curable today and far less contagious than most people think.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Bubonic plague: Yersinia pestis spread by fleas killed perhaps a third of Europe in the Black Death. It still turns up in the American Southwest and is treatable with antibiotics.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Anthrax: Its bacterial spores can survive in soil for decades. Anthrax was one of the first diseases shown to be caused by a specific germ, by Robert Koch.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Scarlet fever: A strep bacterium causes the red rash and 'strawberry tongue'. Once a leading killer of children, antibiotics now cure it easily.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Diphtheria: The bacterium makes a toxin that forms a thick gray membrane in the throat. The 1925 sled-dog serum run to Nome was to fight an outbreak of it.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Influenza: A trap: flu is caused by a virus, so antibiotics do nothing against it. Its surface proteins change often, which is why you need a new shot each year.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Measles: A virus, not a bacterium, and one of the most contagious diseases known. One case can infect around 9 in 10 unvaccinated people nearby.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Malaria: Not a bacterial disease: a single-celled parasite, Plasmodium, spread by Anopheles mosquitoes. It has been a leading killer of humans throughout history.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Athlete's foot: A fungus, not bacteria. The same kind of organism that grows on damp locker-room floors thrives between toes, so antifungal cream is the cure.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Chickenpox: A virus (varicella-zoster), so antibiotics are useless. The same virus stays dormant in nerves and can return decades later as shingles.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Rabies: A virus, not a bacterium. Nearly always fatal once symptoms appear, but Louis Pasteur's 1885 vaccine can prevent it if given soon after a bite.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Polio: A virus that attacks nerves. Vaccines in the 1950s have cut cases by over 99 percent worldwide, leaving it close to eradicated.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Mumps: A virus known for swollen cheeks from inflamed salivary glands. As a virus it does not respond to antibiotics, but the MMR vaccine prevents it.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Ringworm: A trap: there is no worm. It is a fungal skin infection, named for the ring-shaped red rash, and it can spread from pets to people.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Common cold: Caused by hundreds of viruses, rhinoviruses being the most common. That huge variety is why no one has made a vaccine against it.
Diseases caused by bacteria.Shingles: Caused by the chickenpox virus waking up years later. It is a virus, so it's treated with antivirals rather than the antibiotics used for bacteria.

Things bigger than Earth.The Sun: It holds about 99.8 percent of the solar system's mass. Roughly 1.3 million Earths could fit inside it.
Things bigger than Earth.Jupiter: Its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has raged for centuries. All the other planets could fit inside Jupiter.
Things bigger than Earth.Saturn: Its density is less than water, so in a big enough bathtub it would float. Its rings are mostly ice and span far across.
Things bigger than Earth.Uranus: Tilted on its side, probably after an ancient collision, so it rolls around the Sun. It is about four times Earth's width.
Things bigger than Earth.Neptune: It has the fastest winds of any planet, over 2,000 km/h. It was found in 1846 by calculating its position with mathematics first.
Things bigger than Earth.Betelgeuse: A red supergiant in Orion so huge that, set where our Sun is, it would reach past Mars's orbit. It may explode as a supernova someday.
Things bigger than Earth.Sirius: The brightest star in our night sky, about twice the Sun's diameter. Ancient Egyptians based their calendar on its yearly reappearance.
Things bigger than Earth.Milky Way: Our home galaxy contains 100 billion stars or more and is about 100,000 light-years across. We see it edge-on as a pale band.
Things bigger than Earth.Andromeda Galaxy: The nearest big galaxy, 2.5 million light-years away. It's heading toward the Milky Way and will merge with it in billions of years.
Things bigger than Earth.Proxima Centauri: The closest star to the Sun, but a red dwarf only about 1.5 times Jupiter's width. It's still much larger than Earth.
Things bigger than Earth.Orion Nebula: A stellar nursery about 1,300 light-years away, visible to the naked eye as the fuzzy middle 'star' of Orion's sword. Many young stars form there.
Things bigger than Earth.Mars: About half Earth's width. It has the tallest volcano known in the solar system, Olympus Mons, about three times the height of Everest.
Things bigger than Earth.Venus: A trap: it's almost Earth's twin in size, but slightly smaller. A day there lasts longer than its year.
Things bigger than Earth.Mercury: The smallest planet, only a bit bigger than our Moon. It has extreme swings from scorching days to freezing nights.
Things bigger than Earth.The Moon: About a quarter of Earth's width, a huge moon compared to its planet. It drifts about 3.8 cm farther away each year.
Things bigger than Earth.Pluto: Smaller than Earth's Moon. Its heart-shaped icy plain was revealed by the New Horizons flyby in 2015.
Things bigger than Earth.Ganymede: Jupiter's moon is the biggest in the solar system, even larger than Mercury, yet it is still smaller than Earth. It has its own magnetic field.
Things bigger than Earth.Titan: Saturn's largest moon, with a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane. It's still about 40 percent of Earth's width.
Things bigger than Earth.Ceres: The largest object in the asteroid belt, a dwarf planet about 950 km across. It is tiny next to Earth.
Things bigger than Earth.Halley's Comet: Its nucleus is only about 15 km long. It returns about every 76 years, next due in 2061.
Things bigger than Earth.ISS: The space station is about the size of a football field, yet minuscule next to Earth. It orbits roughly 400 km up, circling Earth every 90 minutes.
Things bigger than Earth.Mount Everest: About 8.8 km high, impressive but tiny against Earth's 12,700 km width. It is still growing by a few millimeters a year.
Things bigger than Earth.Pacific Ocean: A trap: the biggest ocean, covering about a third of Earth's surface, yet it is part of Earth, so it can't be bigger.
Things bigger than Earth.Europa: A moon of Jupiter somewhat smaller than our Moon. It hides a salty ocean under its ice, a top place to look for life.

Movies starring Tom Hanks.Captain Phillips: The cast includes Barkhad Abdi, a first-time actor who earned an Oscar nomination as the Somali pirate leader.
Movies starring Tom Hanks.The Terminal: It was inspired by Mehran Karimi Nasseri, an Iranian refugee who lived in Paris's Charles de Gaulle airport for years.
Movies starring Tom Hanks.Sully: It dramatizes the 2009 Hudson River landing, in which all 155 people aboard the US Airways plane survived.
Movies starring Tom Hanks.The Da Vinci Code: Hanks plays symbologist Robert Langdon in the film of Dan Brown's bestseller, which was shot partly inside the Louvre.
Movies starring Tom Hanks.Rain Man: This one stars Dustin Hoffman, who won an Oscar for it, and Tom Cruise as his brother, not Tom Hanks.

Movies starring Tom Hanks.Jerry Maguire: Another Tom, Cruise, played the sports agent who shouted 'Show me the money!'; Hanks wasn't in it.
Movies starring Tom Hanks.Titanic: Hanks wasn't aboard: the leads were Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet, and it tied the record of 11 Oscars.
Movies starring Tom Hanks.Good Will Hunting: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck wrote it and won the screenplay Oscar; Robin Williams won Best Supporting Actor, but Hanks isn't in it.
Movies starring Tom Hanks.The Truman Show: Jim Carrey played the man whose life is a TV show; the role was not Hanks, though he'd have suited its everyman charm.
Movies starring Tom Hanks.Gladiator: Russell Crowe led this Best Picture winner; Hanks wasn't in the cast.
Movies starring Tom Hanks.Ghost: Patrick Swayze and Demi Moore starred, and Whoopi Goldberg won an Oscar, but Hanks wasn't involved.
Movies starring Tom Hanks.Dances with Wolves: Kevin Costner directed, produced and starred in this 1990 Best Picture winner, not Tom Hanks.
Movies starring Tom Hanks.Braveheart: Mel Gibson directed and starred in the 1995 Best Picture winner; Hanks wasn't in it.
Movies starring Tom Hanks.Groundhog Day: Bill Murray plays the weatherman stuck repeating the same day; this classic isn't a Hanks film.

Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Anna: A streak of white hair marks Anna's head after Elsa's magic struck her as a child; Kristen Bell voices her.
Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Olaf: Elsa made Olaf from childhood memories of building a snowman with Anna, and he dreams of experiencing summer.
Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Kristoff: An ice harvester raised by trolls; he often speaks for his reindeer Sven in a goofy voice, saying what the animal would.
Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Sven: Kristoff's reindeer loves carrots and behaves much like a dog, while Kristoff provides his lines in a silly voice.
Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Hans: The charming Prince of the Southern Isles turns out to be the film's villain, a twist many viewers did not expect.
Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Oaken: This trading post owner shouts 'Yoo-hoo!' and sells winter gear, and his shop includes a sauna.
Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Marshmallow: Elsa conjures this giant snow monster to guard her ice palace, and he chases Anna and Kristoff off the mountain.
Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Duke of Weselton: A pompous trade dignitary who sends armed thugs after Elsa; his name is often joked to sound like 'weasel town'.
Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Bruni: A fire-spirit salamander in Frozen II's Enchanted Forest, and one of the four element spirits Elsa meets on her journey.
Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Grand Pabbie: The wise troll leader who raised Kristoff, healed young Anna after Elsa's accident, and erased her memory of the magic.

Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Maximus: Maximus is the palace horse from Tangled who acts more like a bloodhound, and he belongs to another Disney film.

Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Maui: Maui is a demigod from Polynesian myth, voiced by Dwayne Johnson in Moana, and not one of Arendelle's people.
Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Mirabel: Mirabel is the heroine of Encanto, the Colombian family musical, rather than a character from Arendelle.

Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Merida: Merida is from Pixar's Brave, set in Scotland, and is known for her curly red hair and archery.
Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Tiana: Tiana comes from The Princess and the Frog (2009), and was Disney's first Black princess; she lives in New Orleans.
Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Heihei: Heihei is Moana's hopelessly dim rooster from a different Disney film, and he has no place in Arendelle.
Characters in Frozen or Frozen II.Mulan: Mulan is the 1998 Disney heroine based on a Chinese legend, who disguises herself as a soldier.

Sailing terms.Port: The left side of a boat, so named because ships tied up with their left side to the dock, so the steering oar was on the right.
Sailing terms.Starboard: The right side, from the old steering board, an oar mounted on the right side of early ships.
Sailing terms.Bow: The front of the boat, and pronounced to rhyme with cow, unlike the bow of a ribbon or an archer.
Sailing terms.Stern: The back end, where the helm is often found, and it faces back as the boat sails.
Sailing terms.Tack: To turn the bow through the wind, and also the word for the direction a boat is sailing, relative to the wind.
Sailing terms.Jibe: Turning the stern through the wind, which makes the boom swing across fast and can be dangerous.
Sailing terms.Keel: The fin below the hull that keeps the boat from sliding sideways, and on yachts it holds ballast to stop capsizing.
Sailing terms.Mast: The tall pole that holds the sails, and on the biggest tall ships it was made of several sections.
Sailing terms.Boom: The horizontal pole at the bottom of the mainsail, which can hit sailors in an accidental jibe.
Sailing terms.Rudder: The steering blade at the stern, controlled by a tiller or wheel.
Sailing terms.Spinnaker: A big, balloon-shaped sail used when running with the wind, and it's often brightly coloured, helping it to be seen.
Sailing terms.Hull: The body of the boat, and the shape of it determines how fast it can go.
Sailing terms.Jib: A triangular sail at the front of the boat, which helps steer airflow around the main sail.
Sailing terms.Halyard: A rope that hoists a sail up the mast, and the word comes from 'haul yard'.
Sailing terms.Wicket: A cricket term for the stumps, not a nautical term.
Sailing terms.Puck: The disc used in ice hockey, not in sailing.
Sailing terms.Oche: The line from which darts are thrown, which has no use at sea.
Sailing terms.Crease: A cricket term for the lines marking the batter's and bowler's positions.
Sailing terms.Fairway: The mown strip of a golf course between tee and green, though in nautical use, a fairway is a navigable channel.
Sailing terms.Dugout: A shelter for baseball players beside the field, although it also means a canoe made from a hollowed log.
Sailing terms.Saddle: A rider's seat on a horse or bicycle, which has no role on a boat.
Sailing terms.Stirrup: The rider's foot support, though sailors also use the term for a rope footrest under a yard.
Sailing terms.Chairlift: A ski-resort lift that carries skiers uphill, first built in the 1930s, and it is not found on a boat.
Sailing terms.Moguls: The bumps on a ski slope, which skiers navigate in a freestyle event.

WWE wrestling legends.Randy Savage: The Macho Man, known for his gravelly voice and Oooh yeah catchphrase, which was used in Slim Jim ads.
WWE wrestling legends.Ric Flair: The Nature Boy, known for Woooo! and for being one of wrestling's most decorated world champions.
WWE wrestling legends.Triple H: Paul Levesque married Stephanie McMahon, and after retiring became WWE's head of creative.
WWE wrestling legends.Rey Mysterio: A masked luchador who, despite his small size, won the 2006 Royal Rumble and a world title.

WWE wrestling legends.Shawn Michaels: The Heartbreak Kid, nicknamed Mr. WrestleMania for his show-stealing matches, including a famous Ironman match in 1996.

WWE wrestling legends.Conor McGregor: A UFC star who was a two-division champion, not a WWE wrestler.
WWE wrestling legends.Bruce Lee: A martial arts movie legend, never a WWE wrestler.
WWE wrestling legends.Chuck Norris: A karate champion turned action star, not a WWE legend.

WWE wrestling legends.Jackie Chan: A Hong Kong martial arts and action film star.
WWE wrestling legends.Manny Pacquiao: A Filipino boxer who won titles in eight weight divisions.
WWE wrestling legends.Lennox Lewis: A British boxer, the last undisputed heavyweight champion of the 1990s.
WWE wrestling legends.Jet Li: A Chinese wushu champion and film actor.
WWE wrestling legends.Dolph Lundgren: The Swedish actor who played Ivan Drago, not a wrestler.
WWE wrestling legends.Joe Frazier: A boxer who beat Ali in 1971's Fight of the Century.
WWE wrestling legends.Rocky Balboa: A fictional boxer from the Rocky films, played by Stallone. He fought Thunderlips but was never a WWE wrestler.

Places where baseball is hugely popular.USA: Baseball is the national pastime, with the sport's first pro league dating to 1871. The World Series has been played since 1903.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Japan: Baseball has been popular since the 1870s, and Koshien high school tournaments grip the nation. Shohei Ohtani is a global star.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Dominican Republic: A small island nation that sends a huge number of players to the major leagues. Many youngsters train in academies from age 16.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Cuba: Baseball is the national obsession, played since the 1860s. Cuba has won Olympic baseball gold several times.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Venezuela: One of the biggest sources of major league talent. Winter league games draw big crowds, and baseball outranks even football.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.South Korea: The KBO League began in 1982 and is known for passionate cheering and bat flips. Fans chant in sync throughout the game.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Taiwan: Baseball is a unifier here, with the Chinese Professional Baseball League founded in 1990. Taiwan has won Little League World Series titles.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Puerto Rico: A US territory with a long baseball tradition. Roberto Clemente, from here, became the first Latino in the Hall of Fame.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Mexico: Baseball has long been popular, especially in the north. The Mexican League dates from 1925, and Fernando Valenzuela was a national hero.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Nicaragua: Baseball is the top sport, ahead of football. Dennis Martinez, from Nicaragua, became the first from his country in the majors.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Panama: A baseball country that gave the sport Mariano Rivera, the great closer. The sport rivals football in popularity.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.England: The home of cricket and football, and baseball is a curiosity. Rounders, a cousin of baseball, is played in schools.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.India: Cricket rules, with baseball rarely played. The 2008 film Million Dollar Arm told a true story of Indian javelin throwers trying pro baseball.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.France: Baseball has a small following, mostly alongside rugby and football. The French have a league, but few play.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Germany: Football leads. Baseball has a small league and club scene, though it has grown with American bases.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Brazil: Football is everything, and baseball is a niche, mainly among the Japanese-Brazilian community. Brazil has fielded national teams.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Egypt: Football is the national love, and baseball is nearly absent. Some expatriate and school teams exist.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Russia: Ice hockey and football dominate. Baseball has a small following and a league that few know about.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Kenya: Famous for distance running, Kenya has almost no baseball. Rugby and football are the team sports of choice.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Spain: Football comes first, but baseball has a modest following. Spain has a pro league, though few play in it.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Sweden: Winter sports and football hold sway here. Baseball exists in small clubs, mostly as a hobby, and it has never rivaled bandy or hockey.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Ireland: Gaelic football and hurling are the national sports. Baseball is a small interest, mainly among those with American ties.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.Pakistan: Cricket captures the hearts of all. Baseball exists only in a tiny form, despite shared bat-and-ball roots.
Places where baseball is hugely popular.New Zealand: Rugby and cricket lead. Baseball exists locally in a small scene, and softball is also played.

Found in ancient Rome.Aqueduct: Roman aqueducts carried water on gentle slopes over many kilometers, and some, like the one at Segovia, still stand.
Found in ancient Rome.Colosseum: Its arena could be flooded for mock naval battles, and its underground chambers held animals lifted up by lifts.
Found in ancient Rome.Toga: Only male citizens could wear this heavy wool garment. It was hot and awkward, so Romans mostly wore tunics.
Found in ancient Rome.Chariot: Racing at the Circus Maximus drew a crowd of around 150,000 to watch teams in four colors.
Found in ancient Rome.Gladiator: Many gladiators were slaves or prisoners, but some were volunteers. A fighter who won enough could earn a wooden sword and freedom.
Found in ancient Rome.Senate: The council of Rome's elite, which outlived the Republic and the first emperors. The word comes from Latin "senex," meaning old man.
Found in ancient Rome.Forum: The Roman Forum was the heart of public life, home to temples, courts and speeches. The word still means a place for discussion.
Found in ancient Rome.Concrete: Roman concrete used volcanic ash, and structures like the Pantheon's dome, still the biggest unreinforced concrete dome, have lasted nearly 2,000 years.
Found in ancient Rome.Bathhouse: Public baths were social hubs with hot, warm and cold rooms, and a visit cost almost nothing. Some had libraries and gyms.
Found in ancient Rome.Mosaic: Roman floors and walls were covered with tiny stone tiles called tesserae, making pictures from daily life and myth.
Found in ancient Rome.Legion: Rome's main army unit had about 5,000 soldiers and its own eagle standard, and losing that standard was a disgrace.
Found in ancient Rome.Printing press: Not Roman: Gutenberg's press arrived around 1450 in Europe. Romans copied books by hand.
Found in ancient Rome.Gunpowder: Not Roman: invented in China, around the 9th century, and reaching Europe far later.
Found in ancient Rome.Potato: A New World crop from the Andes. Romans never tasted one, since Europeans only met it after 1492.
Found in ancient Rome.Tomato: Native to the Americas, and so absent from Italy until the 1500s. Roman cooking had no tomato sauce.
Found in ancient Rome.Eyeglasses: Invented in Italy only in the late 1200s. Romans used polished gems or water-filled glass to magnify.
Found in ancient Rome.Paper money: Chinese Tang and Song dynasties pioneered it. Romans only used metal coins.
Found in ancient Rome.Chocolate: Cacao came from Mesoamerica, so Romans never tasted chocolate. Europe first saw it in the 1500s.
Found in ancient Rome.Coffee: It reached Europe in the 1600s from the Arab world. Romans drank wine and water, not coffee.
Found in ancient Rome.Maize: Corn was domesticated in Mexico and was unknown in Europe until after Columbus.
Found in ancient Rome.Tobacco: A New World plant, so no Roman smoked a pipe. It arrived in Europe in the 1500s.
Found in ancient Rome.Pumpkin: A New World squash, unknown to Romans, though they did eat other gourds and squashes.
Found in ancient Rome.Chili pepper: Native to the Americas. Romans seasoned with black pepper, imported at great expense from India.
Found in ancient Rome.Vanilla: An orchid native to Mexico, so Romans never flavored anything with it. Aztecs used it to season chocolate.

Titans of Greek myth.Cronus: Leader of the Titans, who overthrew his father Uranus. Fearing the same fate, he swallowed his own children, until Zeus escaped.
Titans of Greek myth.Rhea: Cronus's wife and mother of Zeus, she tricked her husband by giving him a stone wrapped as a baby to swallow instead.
Titans of Greek myth.Oceanus: The Titan of the great river that circled the world, and the oldest of them, he stayed out of the war against Zeus.
Titans of Greek myth.Hyperion: A Titan of heavenly light and father of the sun, moon and dawn. John Keats wrote an unfinished poem about him.
Titans of Greek myth.Atlas: Punished by Zeus to hold up the sky, not the world as often shown. The book of maps takes its name from him.
Titans of Greek myth.Prometheus: He stole fire from the gods for humanity and was chained to a rock, where an eagle ate his liver daily, which regrew.
Titans of Greek myth.Epimetheus: His name means "afterthought," in contrast to his brother Prometheus ("forethought"). He accepted Pandora as his wife, despite warnings.
Titans of Greek myth.Tethys: A Titaness of fresh water, wife of Oceanus. Saturn's moon Tethys is named for her.
Titans of Greek myth.Themis: The Titaness of divine law and order, often depicted holding scales. She's the ancestor of the blindfolded Lady Justice.
Titans of Greek myth.Mnemosyne: The Titaness of memory and mother of the nine Muses by Zeus. The word "mnemonic" comes from her name.
Titans of Greek myth.Iapetus: A Titan whose sons included Prometheus and Atlas. Saturn's moon Iapetus has one dark side and one bright side.
Titans of Greek myth.Coeus: A Titan associated with intellect and inquiry. He's the grandfather of Apollo and Artemis through his daughter Leto.
Titans of Greek myth.Theia: Titaness of sight and shining light. In astronomy, a Mars-sized planet named Theia is thought to have collided with Earth and formed the Moon.
Titans of Greek myth.Zeus: A trap: he led the Olympians, not the Titans. He overthrew them in a ten-year war, the Titanomachy.
Titans of Greek myth.Hera: Zeus's wife and queen of the Olympian gods. She is Cronus's daughter, so a second-generation god, not a Titan.
Titans of Greek myth.Poseidon: Cronus and Rhea's son, so Zeus's brother, an Olympian. The sea god's trident shakes the earth.
Titans of Greek myth.Hades: Another son of Cronus, and thus Olympian generation. He ruled the underworld after drawing lots with his brothers.
Titans of Greek myth.Athena: Born fully armed from Zeus's head, goddess of wisdom and war. An Olympian, not a Titan.
Titans of Greek myth.Apollo: The god of music, sun and prophecy, Zeus's son. His mother Leto was a Titan's daughter, but he's Olympian.
Titans of Greek myth.Cyclops: Zeus's helpers who forged his thunderbolts, they were freed from imprisonment during the Titan war. They are not Titans.
Titans of Greek myth.Heracles: A mortal-born hero, son of Zeus, and not a Titan. He eventually became a god on Olympus.
Titans of Greek myth.Medusa: A mortal Gorgon who was killed by Perseus, from a separate monstrous lineage and not Titan stock.
Titans of Greek myth.Typhon: A monster so fearsome even Zeus fled him at first. He is the child of Gaia and Tartarus, not a Titan.
Titans of Greek myth.Pan: A goat-legged god of shepherds and wild places, whose name gave us "panic." He's a minor god, not a Titan.

Things for making coffee or tea.Kettle: The word kettle comes from Old Norse ketill, meaning cauldron, which suggests how old the idea of boiling water in a pot is.
Things for making coffee or tea.Teapot: Yixing teapots from China are unglazed clay that slowly absorb tea flavor, so devotees brew only one kind in each pot.
Things for making coffee or tea.Coffee grinder: Burr grinders crush beans to an even size, while blade grinders chop unevenly, and uneven grounds brew bitter and weak at once.
Things for making coffee or tea.French press: Despite the name, a coffee press design was patented in Italy in 1929, though the French name is the one that stuck.
Things for making coffee or tea.Sugar bowl: Sugar was a luxury in Europe for centuries, so ornate silver sugar bowls were status symbols at the table.
Things for making coffee or tea.Milk jug: Britons still argue over whether milk goes in the cup before or after the tea.
Things for making coffee or tea.Tea strainer: Tea leaves expand a lot as they steep, and a strainer catches them so you do not drink the leaves.
Things for making coffee or tea.Coffee filter: Melitta Bentz invented the paper coffee filter in 1908 using blotting paper from her son's school notebook.
Things for making coffee or tea.Espresso machine: Angelo Moriondo of Turin patented a steam-driven espresso machine in 1884, long before Italian cafes made it famous.
Things for making coffee or tea.Moka pot: Alfonso Bialetti launched the octagonal aluminum moka pot in 1933, and it remains in kitchens across Italy.
Things for making coffee or tea.Tea infuser: Loose leaves need room to unfurl, and cramped infusers produce weak tea, which is why larger baskets work better.
Things for making coffee or tea.Coffee scoop: A level coffee scoop is traditionally about two tablespoons, the usual dose for a cup of around six ounces.
Things for making coffee or tea.Wok: The wok is built for high-heat stir-frying, with a bowl shape that has nothing to do with brewing a drink.
Things for making coffee or tea.Colander: A colander drains pasta, but its holes are far too large to hold back fine coffee grounds.
Things for making coffee or tea.Grater: The Microplane grew from a woodworking rasp after a home cook used one to zest an orange.
Things for making coffee or tea.Rolling pin: Marble rolling pins stay cool, perfect for pastry but irrelevant when you are boiling water.
Things for making coffee or tea.Cookie cutter: Antique copper cookie cutters are prized by collectors, and they cut dough, not tea leaves.
Things for making coffee or tea.Potato masher: Mashers are used on potatoes and sometimes bananas, but never in a brew.
Things for making coffee or tea.Garlic press: A garlic press forces cloves through tiny holes, a job that has no place in coffee or tea.
Things for making coffee or tea.Pizza cutter: A rolling wheel slices pizza cleanly without dragging the cheese, and it does nothing for your morning drink.
Things for making coffee or tea.Salad spinner: A spinner dries lettuce so dressing clings to the leaves, a different problem from steeping tea.
Things for making coffee or tea.Ladle: A ladle serves soup and punch, but nobody uses one to make a cup of tea or coffee.
Things for making coffee or tea.Corkscrew: Corkscrews are for wine, and the waiter's friend style folds in a little knife for cutting the foil.
Things for making coffee or tea.Cheese slicer: The cheese slicer was invented in 1925 by Norwegian carpenter Thor Bjørklund, who got the idea while slicing with a plane.

Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Rose: Roses are over 30 million years old as a plant lineage, and fossils show they bloomed before humans even existed.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Goes: Goes rhymes with nose even though it is spelled differently; English has dozens of sounds spelled in confusing ways.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Toes: A human foot has 26 bones, and the toes alone make up 14 of them.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Hose: Hose once meant a type of tight leg clothing, like stockings, and only later the garden watering tube.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Those: Those is one of the most common English words, and its th is voiced like the in this, not the th in think.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Froze: Froze is the past tense of freeze, a verb whose forms have changed since Old English, where it was freosan.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Chose: Chose and choose differ in sound: chose rhymes with nose, but choose sounds like booze.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Prose: Prose comes from Latin for straightforward speech, and Moliere's character in a play was shocked to learn he had been speaking it all his life.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Pose: Pose rhymes with nose, and it goes back to Latin pausare, meaning to pause or halt.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Doze: Doze is thought to come from Scandinavian roots and means to sleep lightly, a handy rhyme for nose.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Knows: The silent k in knows was once pronounced; English speakers dropped the k sound around the 1600s but kept the spelling.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Blows: Blows can mean winds or punches, and either way it ends with the same oze sound as nose.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Lose: Lose looks like it rhymes with nose, but it sounds like booze, and it is a frequent spelling mix-up with loose.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Whose: Whose is another trap: despite the o and se it rhymes with booze, not with nose.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Noise: Noise looks close but its oi diphthong makes it rhyme with boys and toys, not with nose.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.News: News ends in an s sound but with a different vowel, and it is plural in spelling, yet we treat it as singular.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Moose: Moose is from an Algonquian word and rhymes with loose, which has the oo sound, not the long o of nose.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Choose: Choose rhymes with booze, while chose with an o rhymes with nose, a frequent mix-up.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Nuts: Nuts begins with n just like nose, and both are classic cases of sound-alike openings that do not rhyme.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Nest: Nest also starts with n and similar letters but ends in st, so the rhyme fails.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Knees: Knees has the ee vowel and rhymes with please and freeze, which are not the same as nose.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Nurse: Nurse starts with n and has an s sound at the end, yet the ur vowel puts it in a different rhyme family.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Shoes: Shoes rhymes with news and blues, which share the oo vowel, and not with nose.
Words that rhyme with 'nose'.Gnaws: Gnaws sounds like nause with an aw vowel, so it rhymes with paws and jaws, not nose.

Facial hair styles.Goatee: The goatee, a tuft on the chin, got its name from its resemblance to a goat's beard, and it has been fashionable since ancient Greece.
Facial hair styles.Mustache: In Victorian Britain, the Royal Navy once required sailors to grow a mustache, and the rule was dropped only in 1916.
Facial hair styles.Sideburns: Sideburns are named for Union General Ambrose Burnside, whose huge side whiskers were first called burnsides.
Facial hair styles.Soul patch: The soul patch, a small tuft under the lower lip, became linked with jazz musicians and beatniks in the 1950s.
Facial hair styles.Handlebar: The handlebar mustache gets its name from the curved handles of bicycles, and the style even has its own world championships.
Facial hair styles.Mutton chops: Mutton chops are bushy sideburns joined across the cheeks, named for the shape of a cut of lamb, and were a Victorian favorite.
Facial hair styles.Stubble: Stubble has a curious name drawn from the stalks left in a farm field after the harvest has been cut.
Facial hair styles.Full beard: A full beard can grow about half an inch a month, and some men keep theirs for life, with the longest topping 17 feet.
Facial hair styles.Van Dyke: The Van Dyke, a pointed beard with a mustache, is named for the 17th-century painter Anthony van Dyck, who portrayed courtiers with it.
Facial hair styles.Chin strap: A chin strap beard is a thin line tracing the jaw and sideburns, which resembles the strap of a helmet.
Facial hair styles.Five o'clock shadow: A five o'clock shadow is the dark stubble visible by late afternoon, and its name goes back to at least the 1930s.
Facial hair styles.Mohawk: Many people link the mohawk to punk culture, but the name comes from a Native American nation, and it is a haircut, not facial hair.
Facial hair styles.Mullet: The mullet, short in front and long in the back, is a hairstyle, and its name was popularized by the Beastie Boys in 1994.
Facial hair styles.Ponytail: A ponytail is a hairstyle, not facial hair, and it is one of the oldest hair arrangements, seen in ancient Greek art.
Facial hair styles.Bun: A bun is hair gathered on the head, not on the face, and ballet dancers have used it for centuries for a tidy look.
Facial hair styles.Pompadour: The pompadour is named for Madame de Pompadour, mistress of Louis XV, and it is a scalp hairstyle.
Facial hair styles.Buzz cut: A buzz cut is hair trimmed short with clippers over the whole head, not facial hair.
Facial hair styles.Bob: The bob, a chin-length cut, became a symbol of independence for women in the 1920s, and it is a head hairstyle.
Facial hair styles.Crew cut: The crew cut got its name from the style of the Yale rowing crew in the 1900s, and it is a hairstyle, not a beard.
Facial hair styles.Pixie cut: The pixie cut, short and cropped, was made famous by Audrey Hepburn in Roman Holiday, but it is hair on the head.
Facial hair styles.Comb-over: A comb-over covers a bald spot by brushing long strands across it, a scalp style rather than facial hair.
Facial hair styles.Bangs: Bangs are hair cut across the forehead, and in British English, they are called a fringe.
Facial hair styles.Undercut: An undercut has shaved sides and longer hair on top, so it belongs to head hair, not facial hair.
Facial hair styles.Beehive: The beehive hairdo, a tall rounded updo, reached its peak in the 1960s and was made famous by Amy Winehouse a generation later.

Things from Cinderella.Glass slipper: In Charles Perrault's 1697 telling the slipper was glass; in the older Grimm version it was gold. Some scholars blame a mistranslation of fur.
Things from Cinderella.Pumpkin carriage: The coach is a pumpkin only for the night: the fairy godmother conjures it from a garden pumpkin, and it turns back at the stroke of twelve.
Things from Cinderella.Fairy godmother: Perrault invented her: earlier versions of the tale had a magic tree or helpful animals granting wishes, not a wand-waving fairy.
Things from Cinderella.Stepsisters: In the Grimm version they slice off toes and heels to squeeze into the slipper, and birds later peck out their eyes.
Things from Cinderella.Midnight: The spell's deadline. Disney's 1950 film made the clock chime famous, and the dash down the palace stairs is the story's best-known chase.
Things from Cinderella.Prince Charming: The prince has no name in the tale; Charming is a title, and he is famously forgettable compared with the heroine who does all the work.
Things from Cinderella.Royal ball: Where the story turns: a ball thrown to find the prince a bride, which in many versions lasts several nights so Cinderella can attend more than once.
Things from Cinderella.Mice: In Disney's film the mice, led by Jaq and Gus, sew her dress and get turned into horses. They are the true workforce of the story.
Things from Cinderella.Stepmother: The villain of nearly every version, and a big reason fairy-tale stepmothers got their bad name. In the Grimms' original the cruelty is far harsher.
Things from Cinderella.Magic wand: The wand is Perrault-era stage magic. In the Grimm version there is no fairy at all; wishes are granted by a tree growing on her mother's grave.
Things from Cinderella.Poisoned apple: Snow White's trap, not Cinderella's. The Queen's poisoned apple is from a different Grimm tale, so it doesn't belong at this ball.
Things from Cinderella.Spinning wheel: That belongs to Sleeping Beauty: Aurora pricks her finger on a spindle. Cinderella's tale has no cursed handiwork.
Things from Cinderella.Beanstalk: Jack and the Beanstalk is an English tale with a giant, not a ball. Different story entirely, despite the shared fairy-tale shelf.
Things from Cinderella.Gingerbread house: Hansel and Gretel stumble on this witch's cottage in the woods. Cinderella's only houses are a cruel household and a palace.
Things from Cinderella.Seven dwarfs: Snow White's companions, named in Disney's film (Doc, Grumpy and the rest). The Grimms' original left the dwarfs nameless.
Things from Cinderella.Red hood: Little Red Riding Hood's famous cloak. Perrault's 1697 version of her tale appeared in the same book as his Cinderella.
Things from Cinderella.Big bad wolf: He belongs to Red Riding Hood and the Three Little Pigs; Cinderella's tale has no talking predators, just mean relatives.
Things from Cinderella.Rapunzel's tower: Rapunzel's tower is in the Grimms' tale, where a witch locks her away. Cinderella's trouble is a kitchen hearth, not a tall prison.
Things from Cinderella.Frog prince: In the Grimms' version, a frog is kissed or thrown against a wall, depending on the edition. Not part of Cinderella's story.
Things from Cinderella.Three bears: Goldilocks' tale, from Robert Southey's 1837 version. In earlier versions the intruder was an old woman, not a girl.
Things from Cinderella.Magic mirror: Snow White's stepmother consults it. Her mirror is the original fashion-police lie detector: it only ever answers truthfully.
Things from Cinderella.Sea witch: Ariel's nemesis Ursula comes from Hans Christian Andersen's The Little Mermaid. Cinderella's helpers are fairy-godmotherly, not oceanic.
Things from Cinderella.Tin soldier: Hans Christian Andersen's steadfast toy, who has one leg and loves a paper dancer. Cinderella's tale is older and has no toy soldiers.
Things from Cinderella.Pea under mattress: Andersen's Princess and the Pea: a real princess feels a pea beneath twenty mattresses. A test of royal sensitivity, not of glass shoes.

Things a jeweler works with.Gold: Pure gold is 24 karat, too soft for most jewelry, so it is alloyed; 18 karat is 75 percent gold.
Things a jeweler works with.Silver: Sterling silver is 92.5 percent pure, mixed with copper for strength, and it tarnishes where sulfur is in the air.
Things a jeweler works with.Platinum: Rarer and denser than gold, it is naturally white and prized for holding gems securely.
Things a jeweler works with.Diamond: A diamond is just carbon, the hardest natural material, yet a sharp blow in the right direction can cleave it.
Things a jeweler works with.Ruby: Rubies are corundum, the same mineral as sapphires, and traces of chromium give them their red.
Things a jeweler works with.Loupe: A small magnifier, typically 10 times, used to inspect stones for flaws.
Things a jeweler works with.Pearl: The only gem made by living creatures, built when an oyster layers nacre around an irritant.
Things a jeweler works with.Emerald: Emeralds so often have internal flaws that jewelers call them their jardin, French for garden.
Things a jeweler works with.Sapphire: Sapphires come in every color except red; a red one is a ruby.
Things a jeweler works with.Solder: An alloy that melts at a lower temperature than the metal it joins, and jewelers choose between hard, medium and easy grades.
Things a jeweler works with.Ring mandrel: A tapered rod marked with sizes, used to shape and size rings.
Things a jeweler works with.Granite: A hard igneous rock, more typical of kitchen countertops than of jewelry.
Things a jeweler works with.Concrete: A mix of cement, sand, gravel and water, so a builder's material, not a jeweler's.
Things a jeweler works with.Asphalt: Natural asphalt lakes exist, like Pitch Lake in Trinidad, but it paves roads, not rings.
Things a jeweler works with.Plywood: Thin wood veneers glued crosswise for strength, a carpenter's product.
Things a jeweler works with.Cardboard: Jewelry boxes may use it, but it is a packaging material, not a jeweler's work metal.
Things a jeweler works with.Drywall: Gypsum plaster pressed between sheets of paper, for walls.
Things a jeweler works with.Gravel: Gold is sometimes panned from river gravel, but a jeweler does not work with gravel itself.
Things a jeweler works with.Tarmac: Named for tarmacadam, the road surface, and now also used for airport aprons.
Things a jeweler works with.Brick: Babylon's Ishtar Gate glittered in glazed blue bricks, yet bricks belong to builders, not jewelers.
Things a jeweler works with.Cinder block: A hollow concrete block for walls, nothing like fine jewelry stone.
Things a jeweler works with.Fiberglass: Glass fibers in resin make boats and insulation, not jewelry.
Things a jeweler works with.Rebar: Steel reinforcing bars sit inside concrete, not inside rings.
Things a jeweler works with.Tar: Sticky black stuff from coal or pine, and no jeweler works with it.

Things on an invoice.Invoice number: A unique number lets a business track every bill and spot a missing one; many countries legally require invoices to be numbered in sequence.
Things on an invoice.Due date: Many invoices are due in 30 days, and late payers may face interest; some companies offer a small discount for paying early.
Things on an invoice.Total amount: The bottom line is the figure that matters, and it must equal the line items plus tax, or the accountant will be calling.
Things on an invoice.Sales tax: In the EU this is VAT, and invoices usually must show it as a separate line so businesses can reclaim it.
Things on an invoice.Line items: Each line describes one product or service, which makes it easy to dispute a single charge without rejecting the whole bill.
Things on an invoice.Payment terms: Shorthand like "net 30" means full payment is due 30 days after the invoice date, and "2/10 net 30" adds a 2 percent early discount.
Things on an invoice.Billing address: It tells the buyer's accounts department where to send the bill, and it can differ from where the goods were shipped.
Things on an invoice.Company name: A legal business name on an invoice matters for tax records, so it must match the registered company, not just its trading brand.
Things on an invoice.Bank details: Fraudsters sometimes send fake invoices or change bank details, so careful companies call to confirm any change in account numbers.
Things on an invoice.Unit price: It is the cost of one item, multiplied by the quantity, and discounts are often applied by changing this number.
Things on an invoice.Blood type: A hospital record has it, but a bill does not, even though your type (A, B, AB or O) can matter for transfusions.
Things on an invoice.Star sign: Western astrology has twelve signs, with no place on a bill; the sign you are depends only on which date you were born.
Things on an invoice.Weather forecast: Forecasts are probabilities; a 70 percent chance of rain means rain is expected at some point across about 70 percent of the area.
Things on an invoice.Recipe: Recipes are not protected by copyright in many countries, though the writing and photos around them are, and none belong on an invoice.
Things on an invoice.Horoscope: Daily horoscopes are written to be vague enough to fit almost anyone, a trick called the Barnum effect.
Things on an invoice.Lottery numbers: Every number combination is equally likely, so the draw 1-2-3-4-5-6 has exactly the same chance as any other.
Things on an invoice.Shoe size: Sizes differ around the world, and the British scale is based on barleycorns, each one third of an inch long.
Things on an invoice.Movie rating: Ratings like G and PG come from industry boards, and the US film rating system began in 1968 to replace the older Hays Code.
Things on an invoice.Song lyrics: Lyrics are protected by copyright, so printing them on a flyer without permission can be a legal problem.
Things on an invoice.Calorie count: A food calorie is really a kilocalorie, the energy to heat a kilogram of water by one degree Celsius.
Things on an invoice.Pet's name: It may appear on a vet bill, but a company invoice has no use for it, even if fluffy is the most important client.
Things on an invoice.Password: Never put one on an invoice, because the document gets emailed around and stored, which makes it a security risk.
Things on an invoice.Bedtime: Teenagers' body clocks really do shift later, a biological change rather than laziness, which is why early school starts are controversial.
Things on an invoice.Joke of the day: Humor has no place on formal paperwork, though some small businesses do add a friendly note at the bottom.
