Apple-owned software and apps.GarageBand: Launched free with new Macs in 2004; Grimes recorded her album Visions with it.
Apple-owned software and apps.iMovie: Debuted in 1999 on the iMac DV and made home video editing accessible, long before smartphones.
Apple-owned software and apps.Keynote: Made for Steve Jobs's own keynote presentations before Apple released it to the public.
Apple-owned software and apps.Pages: Apple's word processor, part of iWork, which can also open and export Word documents.
Apple-owned software and apps.Numbers: A spreadsheet app with a free-form canvas, rather than the usual endless grid.
Apple-owned software and apps.Safari: Apple's browser, released in 2003 and built on the KHTML engine that became WebKit, which Chrome originally used.
Apple-owned software and apps.Xcode: The development environment required to build Apple apps, and it's free in the Mac App Store.
Apple-owned software and apps.Shazam: Apple bought it in 2018; in the UK it began as a service where you dialed 2580 to identify songs.
Apple-owned software and apps.iTunes: Launched in 2001 as a music player and later became a store; Apple retired it in 2019.
Apple-owned software and apps.FaceTime: Introduced in 2010 with the iPhone 4, whose video calling Jobs promised would be an open standard.
Apple-owned software and apps.Siri: Began as a spin-off from SRI International; Apple bought it in 2010 and added it to the iPhone 4S in 2011.
Apple-owned software and apps.Photoshop: Adobe's image editor and the standard for photo retouching, nothing to do with Apple's own apps.
Apple-owned software and apps.Premiere Pro: Adobe's video editor, which is Final Cut Pro's biggest rival.
Apple-owned software and apps.Excel: Microsoft's spreadsheet program, which also runs on the Mac but isn't Apple's.
Apple-owned software and apps.Word: Microsoft's word processor, which dominates offices; Apple's rival is Pages.
Apple-owned software and apps.PowerPoint: Microsoft's presentation software, and Keynote's rival.
Apple-owned software and apps.Chrome: Google's browser, built on the Blink engine that began as a fork of Safari's WebKit.
Apple-owned software and apps.Firefox: Mozilla's independent browser, descended from the old Netscape code.
Apple-owned software and apps.Audacity: A free, open-source audio editor first released in 2000.
Apple-owned software and apps.Ableton Live: A Berlin-made music production program from 2001, popular with electronic musicians.
Apple-owned software and apps.FL Studio: A Belgian music tool, formerly known as FruityLoops, for beatmakers.
Apple-owned software and apps.Zoom: A video-call service that took off during the pandemic, not owned by Apple.

Invented in Japan.Walkman: Sony's 1979 TPS-L2 let people carry music with them, and it was reportedly requested by co-founder Masaru Ibuka for his flights.
Invented in Japan.Emoji: Shigetaka Kurita designed the first 176 in 1999 for NTT DoCoMo's mobile internet, and New York's MoMA now holds the originals.
Invented in Japan.QR code: Denso Wave engineer Masahiro Hara invented it in 1994 to track car parts, and was said to have been inspired by black and white Go stones.
Invented in Japan.Tamagotchi: Bandai's 1996 egg-shaped digital pet sold over 80 million units, and it taught a generation about the guilt of a neglected toy.
Invented in Japan.Game Boy: Gunpei Yokoi designed it with older, cheaper tech, and its 1989 launch bundle with Tetris helped sell over 100 million handhelds.
Invented in Japan.VHS: JVC's Video Home System beat Sony's Betamax in the 1980s, partly because it could record longer, and the format lasted into the 2000s.
Invented in Japan.Rice cooker: Toshiba released the first practical automatic electric model in 1955, and it solved the problem of watching a pot.
Invented in Japan.Bullet train: The Tokaido Shinkansen opened in 1964, just before the Tokyo Olympics, and it has never had a passenger fatality due to a crash or derailment.
Invented in Japan.Blue LED: Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura earned the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics for it, and it made white LED lighting possible.
Invented in Japan.PlayStation: Sony built it in the early 1990s after a failed deal with Nintendo, and it helped turn CD-based consoles into the norm.
Invented in Japan.Telephone: Alexander Graham Bell patented it in 1876 in the US, and some would credit Antonio Meucci with earlier work.
Invented in Japan.iPhone: Apple created it in California in 2007, though many of its parts come from Japanese suppliers.
Invented in Japan.Light bulb: Thomas Edison made it practical in the US around 1879, and the same year Joseph Swan was demonstrating his own in Britain.
Invented in Japan.World Wide Web: Tim Berners-Lee proposed it at CERN in Switzerland in 1989, and it is not the same as the internet.
Invented in Japan.Computer mouse: Douglas Engelbart's team at Stanford Research Institute built the first in the 1960s, and it had a wooden shell.
Invented in Japan.Microwave oven: American engineer Percy Spencer noticed it at Raytheon in the 1940s, and the first ones were as big as a fridge.
Invented in Japan.Typewriter: Early commercial machines are credited to Americans like Christopher Latham Sholes, whose QWERTY layout is still used.
Invented in Japan.Phonograph: Thomas Edison invented it in 1877, and the first recording was reportedly of him reciting Mary Had a Little Lamb.
Invented in Japan.Transistor: Bell Labs scientists in New Jersey made it in 1947, and they got the 1956 Nobel for it.
Invented in Japan.Email: Ray Tomlinson sent the first network email in 1971 and picked the at sign for addresses.
Invented in Japan.GPS: The US military built it, and satellites went up from the 1970s, so Japan did not invent it.
Invented in Japan.Barcode: It was dreamed up on a Miami beach by Norman Woodland, who traced lines in the sand, and the first scan was a pack of gum in 1974.
Invented in Japan.Wi-Fi: Australian CSIRO researchers helped with its key technology in the 1990s, and the name does not stand for anything.
Invented in Japan.Bluetooth: Ericsson of Sweden created it, and its name honors the Viking king Harald Bluetooth, who united Denmark.

Legendary Pokémon.Mewtwo: Created in a lab as a clone of Mew, it was the final boss of the original Red and Blue games, hidden in Cerulean Cave.
Legendary Pokémon.Lugia: Guardian of the sea in Silver, it lives in the Whirl Islands, and its wings are said to cause storms for 40 days.
Legendary Pokémon.Ho-Oh: The rainbow phoenix of Gold, said to appear to those with a pure heart, and it can revive fallen Pokemon.
Legendary Pokémon.Rayquaza: A sky dragon that lives in the ozone layer, it calms the legendary clash of Kyogre and Groudon in Emerald.
Legendary Pokémon.Kyogre: The sea legend on the cover of Sapphire is said to have expanded the oceans in ancient times, and fights Groudon.
Legendary Pokémon.Groudon: The land legend of Ruby, said to have raised continents, and doomed to a battle with Kyogre over the world's balance.
Legendary Pokémon.Dialga: The time deity of Diamond, said to control time itself, and the first of the Sinnoh creation duo with Palkia.
Legendary Pokémon.Palkia: The space deity of Pearl, it is said to control the dimensions of space, and rival to Dialga.
Legendary Pokémon.Zapdos: One of the original three legendary birds, it crackles with electricity and is said to live in thunderclouds.
Legendary Pokémon.Articuno: The ice bird of Kanto's legendary trio is said to appear to lost people in snowy mountains.
Legendary Pokémon.Moltres: The fire bird among the three Kanto legends, said to blaze brighter when wounded, and it uses flames to heal.
Legendary Pokémon.Giratina: Banished to the Distortion World for its violence, it is the cover legendary of Platinum, and can change forms.
Legendary Pokémon.Zekrom: The dark dragon of Black, the ideals counterpart to Reshiram's truth, and mascot of Pokemon Black.
Legendary Pokémon.Pikachu: Pikachu is the franchise's mascot and Ash's partner, but it's an ordinary Electric mouse, available early in Viridian Forest.
Legendary Pokémon.Charizard: Charizard is among the most iconic Pokemon and top trading card, but it evolves from Charmander so it's not legendary.
Legendary Pokémon.Snorlax: A huge sleeper that blocks roads in the games until you wake it; powerful and rare, but not a legendary.
Legendary Pokémon.Gyarados: A fierce sea serpent that evolves from the feeble Magikarp, which is a dramatic transformation but not a legendary.
Legendary Pokémon.Dragonite: A pseudo-legendary, with 600 base stats, but it evolves from Dratini, so the game doesn't classify it as legendary.
Legendary Pokémon.Lucario: A Fighting and Steel Pokemon with aura powers; it evolves from Riolu, which excludes it from the legendary class.
Legendary Pokémon.Gengar: A ghost that evolves from Haunter via trade; despite its popularity, it isn't legendary.
Legendary Pokémon.Eevee: Famous for branching evolutions, Eevee is common enough that some trainers get one as a gift; not legendary.
Legendary Pokémon.Garchomp: A pseudo-legendary dragon with 600 base stats, but it evolves from Gible, so it isn't a true legendary.
Legendary Pokémon.Tyranitar: A pseudo-legendary, evolving from Larvitar; strong enough to rival legends but classified as normal.
Legendary Pokémon.Metagross: A pseudo-legendary Steel and Psychic with 600 base stats, evolving from Beldum, so not a true legendary.

Italian Renaissance painters.Leonardo da Vinci: The creator of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper also filled notebooks with inventions and anatomical drawings.
Italian Renaissance painters.Michelangelo: He painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling, mostly standing, and considered himself primarily a sculptor.
Italian Renaissance painters.Raphael: His School of Athens fresco in the Vatican gathers the great philosophers, with Plato resembling Leonardo.
Italian Renaissance painters.Botticelli: His Birth of Venus shows the goddess rising from a shell and is one of the most famous paintings in the world.
Italian Renaissance painters.Titian: A Venetian master known for his glowing reds, and a long career spanning nearly seventy years.
Italian Renaissance painters.Tintoretto: His nickname means 'little dyer', after his father's trade, and his dramatic, rapidly painted scenes lit up Venice.
Italian Renaissance painters.Veronese: A Venetian known for huge lavish banquet scenes, one of which, Wedding at Cana, hangs opposite the Mona Lisa in the Louvre.
Italian Renaissance painters.Masaccio: His frescoes in Florence's Brancacci Chapel introduced realistic perspective and weight, and he died young at about 27.
Italian Renaissance painters.Fra Angelico: A Dominican friar whose painting was so serene that he was later declared a blessed, and called 'Angelic'.
Italian Renaissance painters.Mantegna: His foreshortened Lamentation over the Dead Christ is an early masterpiece of dramatic perspective.
Italian Renaissance painters.Giovanni Bellini: A Venetian painter famed for soft color and for the Pesaro altarpiece, and Mantegna's brother-in-law.
Italian Renaissance painters.Perugino: Raphael's teacher in Umbria is best known for painting Christ handing the keys to Saint Peter in the Sistine Chapel.
Italian Renaissance painters.Caravaggio: Caravaggio is Baroque, born after the Renaissance, famous for dramatic light and shadow.
Italian Renaissance painters.Rembrandt: A Dutch Golden Age master, not Italian, famous for portraits and the Night Watch.
Italian Renaissance painters.Vermeer: A Dutch painter, not Italian, famous for the Girl with a Pearl Earring.
Italian Renaissance painters.Rubens: A Flemish Baroque painter known for lush, fleshy figures, not Italian.
Italian Renaissance painters.Goya: A Spanish painter from a later era, the court painter who turned dark and haunting.
Italian Renaissance painters.Velázquez: A Spanish court painter of the Baroque, who painted Las Meninas.
Italian Renaissance painters.Albrecht Dürer: A German Renaissance master, not Italian, famous for his engravings.
Italian Renaissance painters.Jan van Eyck: A Flemish painter of the 1400s who helped perfect oil painting, and painted the Arnolfini Portrait.
Italian Renaissance painters.Canaletto: A Venetian painter of the 1700s known for city views, far later than the Renaissance.
Italian Renaissance painters.Modigliani: An Italian painter of the 20th century, famed for elongated faces and necks.
Italian Renaissance painters.Monet: A French Impressionist, far from the Italian Renaissance, famed for water lilies.
Italian Renaissance painters.J. M. W. Turner: An English Romantic landscape painter known for stormy seas and light.

Literary villains.Iago: Shakespeare gives Othello's scheming ensign more lines than Othello himself, and he never fully explains his motive.
Literary villains.Moriarty: Conan Doyle created him in 1893 mainly to kill Holmes off, then had to bring Holmes back after public outcry.
Literary villains.Count Dracula: Stoker took the name from a book about Wallachia, where a medieval prince was called Dracula.
Literary villains.Voldemort: His name suggests 'flight of death', and 'Tom Marvolo Riddle' is an anagram of 'I am Lord Voldemort'.
Literary villains.Sauron: Tolkien's Dark Lord is never seen in physical form during the story, appearing only as a burning Eye.
Literary villains.The White Witch: Jadis keeps Narnia in endless winter, with Christmas never coming, and in The Magician's Nephew she is revealed to come from the dead world of Charn.
Literary villains.Captain Hook: Barrie made the pirate an Old Etonian, so he cares about good form even in his last moments.
Literary villains.Mrs. Danvers: The housekeeper of Manderley worships the dead Rebecca and tries to drive the new wife to suicide.
Literary villains.Bill Sikes: Oliver Twist's brutal burglar is accompanied by his dog Bull's-eye, and the murder of Nancy was the novel's most shocking scene.
Literary villains.Big Brother: Orwell's tyrant in 1984 gave his name to a TV format; the real 'big brother' is a face on posters, never met.
Literary villains.Cruella de Vil: She first appeared in Dodie Smith's 1956 novel, and her name suggests both 'cruel' and 'devil'.
Literary villains.Miss Trunchbull: Roald Dahl's headmistress is a former Olympic hammer thrower who swings children by their pigtails.
Literary villains.Dolores Umbridge: In pink cardigans and with kitten plates, this villain is defined by petty bureaucratic cruelty, not dark magic.
Literary villains.Nurse Ratched: Ken Kesey's tyrannical ward nurse in One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest won Louise Fletcher an Oscar on screen.
Literary villains.Atticus Finch: He is the novel's hero in To Kill a Mockingbird, though the later Go Set a Watchman showed him with racist views.
Literary villains.Frodo Baggins: The Ring-bearer is the hero of The Lord of the Rings, who carries the villain's weapon to destroy it.
Literary villains.Aslan: Aslan is Narnia's rightful king and creator, a heroic lion whom Lewis intended as a Christ-like figure, not a villain.
Literary villains.Peter Pan: Barrie calls Peter 'gay and innocent and heartless', but he's the story's hero, defending the Lost Boys against Hook.
Literary villains.Sherlock Holmes: The hero detective never actually says 'Elementary, my dear Watson' in the original stories.
Literary villains.Elizabeth Bennet: Austen's heroine begins Pride and Prejudice by wrongly judging Darcy, but she is no villain.
Literary villains.Jane Eyre: Brontë's heroine is the hero; the madwoman in the attic is a victim, more tragic than villainous.
Literary villains.Matilda: Matilda is the child hero who outwits Miss Trunchbull, discovering she can move objects with her mind.
Literary villains.Gandalf: Gandalf's name comes from Old Norse and means roughly 'wand-elf'; he's the wise ally of the heroes, not a villain.
Literary villains.Jo March: Louisa May Alcott modeled Jo on herself; the aspiring writer is the heroine of Little Women, not a villain.

Things that break easily.Egg: An eggshell is surprisingly strong under even, end-to-end pressure thanks to its dome shape, but a small sharp tap along its side cracks it.
Things that break easily.Wine glass: A singer's pure sustained note at the glass's resonant frequency can make it vibrate until it shatters, which is why the party trick works.
Things that break easily.Light bulb: Thomas Edison's team tested thousands of materials for the filament, and the thin glass envelope around it is a vacuum or inert gas that implodes easily.
Things that break easily.Glass ornament: Blown-glass Christmas baubles became a tradition in Lauscha, Germany, in the 1800s, where glassblowers first shaped them by hand.
Things that break easily.Porcelain vase: True porcelain is fired at around 1,300 degrees Celsius, making it hard yet brittle, and Chinese kilns perfected it over a thousand years ago.
Things that break easily.Mirror: A mirror is just glass with a thin metal coating, usually silver or aluminum, on the back, and a cracked one is a sheet of fragile glass.
Things that break easily.Soap bubble: A bubble is a thin water film sandwiched between soap layers, and it pops when evaporation thins one spot of the film too far.
Things that break easily.Snowflake: Each snowflake is a delicate ice crystal with six-fold symmetry, and it melts or breaks apart at the lightest touch of a warm fingertip.
Things that break easily.Potato chip: The crisp was said to be invented in 1853 at a Saratoga Springs restaurant, supposedly to annoy a customer who sent his fries back as too thick.
Things that break easily.China teacup: Fine bone china contains ash from cattle bones, which makes it surprisingly strong and translucent despite looking dainty.
Things that break easily.Icicle: Icicles grow as meltwater drips and refreezes, and a typical one can snap off and fall at a speed that makes it genuinely dangerous overhead.
Things that break easily.Dried leaf: Autumn leaves turn crisp because a layer at the stem seals off, cutting off water; once dry, the thin tissue crumbles at a touch.
Things that break easily.Anvil: Blacksmiths' anvils are forged of hardened steel and weigh over a hundred kilograms, so they stay put under thousands of hammer strikes.
Things that break easily.Bowling ball: Modern balls are made of polyurethane or resin around a dense core, tough enough to survive years of striking pins at 15 miles per hour.
Things that break easily.Brick: Fired clay bricks have been used for over 5,000 years, and good ones withstand centuries of weather and loads when stacked in walls.
Things that break easily.Rubber ball: Rubber's elasticity lets it absorb impact by deforming and snapping back, so a dropped ball bounces instead of breaking.
Things that break easily.Steel beam: Steel bends and deforms under extreme loads before it fails, which is why skyscrapers use it to give warning rather than shatter suddenly.
Things that break easily.Car tire: Tires are layered with steel wire and fabric under rubber, built to flex all day over potholes and rubble without cracking.
Things that break easily.Hammer: The hammer is one of the oldest tools, with stone versions about three million years old, and a steel head is made to take repeated blows.
Things that break easily.Cast iron pan: A cast iron pan can last for generations, though a hard blow on a hard floor can crack it, because cast iron is strong but somewhat brittle.
Things that break easily.Rock: A rock is a trap here: granite can be extremely durable, though sharp impacts can fracture some brittle stones along natural weak planes.
Things that break easily.Leather boot: Leather is tanned animal hide, and a well-kept pair of boots can be resoled and worn for decades.
Things that break easily.Wool sweater: Wool fibers are crimped like tiny springs, so they stretch and rebound instead of snapping, and a sweater can bend endlessly without damage.
Things that break easily.Pillow: A pillow is soft and shapeless, so nothing about a fall or squeeze can break it, and its filling just fluffs back into place.

Add 'port' to make a word.Pass: A passport proves your identity abroad, and the word is thought to come from permission to pass through a port.
Add 'port' to make a word.Sup: To support is to bear weight or give backing, and the word is built from the Latin sub, under, and portare, to carry.
Add 'port' to make a word.Re: Report comes from Latin reportare, to carry back, which fits what a reporter does with news.
Add 'port' to make a word.Ex: To export is to carry goods out of a country, and trade in goods and services accounts for a big share of the world economy.
Add 'port' to make a word.Im: To import is to bring goods in from abroad, and Latin portare, to carry, gives both import and export.
Add 'port' to make a word.Trans: Transport comes from Latin for carry across, and the same root shows up in portable and porter.
Add 'port' to make a word.Rap: Rapport means a harmonious bond, and it came from the French verb rapporter, to bring back.
Add 'port' to make a word.De: To deport means to send someone out of a country, and its root is Latin for carry away.
Add 'port' to make a word.Ship: Shipport isn't a word, though ships certainly dock at ports, and the trap is how naturally the two fit together.
Add 'port' to make a word.Bus: Busport isn't a word in English, even though buses use stations, and Bus itself is short for omnibus, meaning for all.
Add 'port' to make a word.Train: Trainport isn't a word, though stations are common; 'port' attaches to air and sea travel instead.
Add 'port' to make a word.Boat: Boatport isn't a word, but a boat reaches a harbor, which is a kind of port.
Add 'port' to make a word.Plane: Planeport isn't a word; the usual term is airport, which swaps plane for air.
Add 'port' to make a word.Bike: Bikeport isn't a real word, even though bikes can be parked, and a rack is the usual term.
Add 'port' to make a word.Truck: Truckport isn't a word, though lorries and trucks do use ports for loading and unloading cargo.
Add 'port' to make a word.Road: Roadport isn't a word, and roads and ports are linked since trucks carry cargo from one to the other.

Things at a gas station.Fuel pump: Modern fuel pumps shut off automatically when the tank is full, thanks to a small air-sensing hole in the nozzle.
Things at a gas station.Nozzle: The nozzle's automatic shut-off works through suction from the fuel flow, which gets blocked when fuel reaches the tank's neck.
Things at a gas station.Air pump: Air pumps let drivers top up tyres; correct pressure improves fuel economy and reduces tyre wear.
Things at a gas station.Car wash: Many stations have a car wash, which first appeared in Detroit in 1914 and was run by hand.
Things at a gas station.Convenience store: Many filling stations now earn more from the convenience store than from fuel.
Things at a gas station.Diesel: Rudolf Diesel showed his engine at the 1900 Paris World's Fair running on peanut oil.
Things at a gas station.Unleaded: Unleaded petrol replaced leaded fuel, which had tetraethyl lead added in the 1920s to stop engine knock.
Things at a gas station.Canopy: The canopy keeps drivers dry while they fill up, and is lit brightly so the station is easily seen at night.
Things at a gas station.Squeegee: The squeegee is the rubber-bladed tool kept in a bucket at the pump, so drivers can wipe the windscreen clean.
Things at a gas station.Attendant: Attendants are rare in some places; in New Jersey, self-service fuelling has long been banned, so an attendant must pump your gas.
Things at a gas station.Jerry can: The jerry can was a German design from the 1930s that Allies copied after finding it superior to their own.
Things at a gas station.Runway: A runway is for aircraft; a gas station's forecourt is for cars, though both involve fuel.
Things at a gas station.Moat: A moat is a ditch around a castle, and gas stations don't have them.
Things at a gas station.Altar: An altar is found in a church, not at a gas station.
Things at a gas station.Pew: A pew is a church bench; you won't find one at a gas station.
Things at a gas station.Hayloft: A hayloft is a barn feature, not a gas station fixture.
Things at a gas station.Ballroom: A ballroom is for dancing; a gas station is for fuelling.
Things at a gas station.Stage curtain: A stage curtain belongs to theatres, and gas stations have no performances.
Things at a gas station.Gangplank: A gangplank is for boarding a ship, not for filling up a car.
Things at a gas station.Trapeze: A trapeze is circus gear, and not found at a gas station.
Things at a gas station.Ski lift: A ski lift is for mountains, and the nearest thing at a gas station is a car lift in the garage.
Things at a gas station.Dugout: A dugout is where baseball players sit, and not part of a gas station.
Things at a gas station.Chandelier: A chandelier is an ornate hanging light for grand rooms, and gas stations use fluorescent or LED lights.
Things at a gas station.Sandpit: A sandpit is for children's play and not found at gas stations.

Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Batwing: Batman's bat-shaped jet appeared in the comics from the 1940s, but Tim Burton's 1989 film made its wide black wings iconic.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Batcycle: Batman's motorcycle, often shown with a sidecar for Robin in older stories, proves the Dark Knight's garage holds more than one car.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Batboat: A speedboat for chasing criminals across Gotham's harbor, it appeared in the comics in the 1940s and starred in the 1966 TV movie.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Invisible Jet: Wonder Woman's transparent plane lets her fly unseen; fans have joked for decades about how she can find the pilot's seat.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Quinjet: The Avengers' supersonic jet is named for its five engines; it can hover like a helicopter and has carried the team since the 1960s.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Fantasticar: The Fantastic Four's flying car, built by Reed Richards, can split into separate pieces, one for each member of the team.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Helicarrier: S.H.I.E.L.D.'s airborne aircraft carrier floats on huge engines and fans; Nick Fury's mobile base was introduced in Marvel's Ultimate comics before the films.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.X-Jet: The X-Men's Blackbird jet is modeled on the real SR-71 Blackbird spy plane, a craft that really could fly above Mach 3.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Mystery Machine: The Scooby-Doo gang's psychedelic van is a cartoon vehicle, not a superhero ride; Mystery Inc. unmasks crooks rather than fights with powers.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.KITT: The talking black Pontiac Trans Am from Knight Rider is a TV car, so it fits crime-fighters on screen but not comic book heroes.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Herbie: This sentient Volkswagen Beetle with racing number 53 is a Disney movie star, not a vehicle belonging to any comic superhero.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Ecto-1: The Ghostbusters' converted 1959 Cadillac ambulance is a film vehicle; the team are scientists with proton packs, not comic superheroes.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.DeLorean: The time machine from Back to the Future used a real car whose stainless-steel body was left unpainted; only about 9,000 were made.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Millennium Falcon: Han Solo's freighter made the Kessel Run in under twelve parsecs, a line that confuses people since a parsec measures distance, not time.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.TARDIS: The Doctor's time machine is bigger on the inside and disguised as a 1960s British police box, a design that was already outdated when the show began.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Mach 5: Speed Racer's car in the anime is a racing machine with a button-operated gadget set, not a superhero's transport.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Thunderbird 2: The green transport craft of International Rescue in Thunderbirds is puppet-show hardware, so it belongs to a rescue organization rather than caped heroes.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Lightning McQueen: The red race car star of Pixar's Cars carries number 95, a nod to the year Toy Story, Pixar's first film, was released in 1995.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Planet Express: The delivery ship in Futurama is owned by a courier company, not a superhero, and its crew mostly bumble through missions.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Magic School Bus: Ms. Frizzle's shape-shifting bus takes children on science trips; it's an educational cartoon vehicle, not a hero's craft.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Knight Bus: This triple-decker purple bus rescues stranded witches and wizards in Harry Potter, though its name has nothing to do with comic book knights.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Hogwarts Express: The scarlet steam train to Hogwarts leaves from platform 9 and three-quarters; the film locomotive was really a 1937 GWR Hall class engine.
Vehicles used by comic book superheroes.Snowspeeder: The Rebel Alliance's Hoth airspeeder in The Empire Strikes Back took down AT-ATs with tow cables, but Star Wars is not a comic book superhero setting.

Sunglasses styles.Aviator: Ray-Ban created this teardrop shape in 1937 for US Air Corps pilots, to cut glare in the sky.
Sunglasses styles.Wayfarer: Ray-Ban's 1952 Wayfarer was one of the first plastic frames, and it became a style classic through the 1960s.
Sunglasses styles.Cat-eye: Pointed up at the corners, the 1950s cat-eye frame is linked with starlets and still looks glamorous.
Sunglasses styles.Round: Tiny round lenses were John Lennon's signature, which is why many call them Lennon glasses.
Sunglasses styles.Wraparound: These curve around the face to block light from the side, and Oakley made them popular for sports.
Sunglasses styles.Clubmaster: Its browline frame mixes plastic on top and metal below, a 1950s Ray-Ban design.
Sunglasses styles.Shield: This is a single large lens across both eyes, a futuristic style from the 1980s ski and cycling scene.
Sunglasses styles.Oversized: Large frames cover much of the face, and Jackie Kennedy and Audrey Hepburn are linked with them.
Sunglasses styles.Mirrored: A reflective coating bounces light away from the lens and hides the wearer's eyes.
Sunglasses styles.Bifocal: Bifocals were invented by Benjamin Franklin, who got tired of swapping glasses; they are for reading, not shade.
Sunglasses styles.Monocle: A monocle is a single lens held by the eye socket, not a sun-blocking style.
Sunglasses styles.Pince-nez: The pince-nez grips the nose with a spring, worn by Chekhov and Theodore Roosevelt, but not tinted for sun.
Sunglasses styles.Contact lens: A contact lens sits on the eye, and the first glass ones were made in the 1880s.
Sunglasses styles.Lorgnette: A lorgnette is a pair of glasses on a handle, a fancy item for opera-goers and not for shade.
Sunglasses styles.Magnifying glass: A magnifying glass enlarges, which is the opposite of what sunglasses do.
Sunglasses styles.Opera glasses: Opera glasses are small binoculars for the theater, with no tint at all.
Sunglasses styles.Binoculars: Binoculars bring faraway things closer, they do not shade your eyes.
Sunglasses styles.Periscope: A periscope lets submarines see above the surface, with mirrors at each end.
Sunglasses styles.Telescope: Telescopes first appeared in the Netherlands in 1608, and Galileo's version made them famous.
Sunglasses styles.Kaleidoscope: The kaleidoscope was invented by Scottish scientist David Brewster in 1816, who patented it.
Sunglasses styles.Loupe: A loupe is a jeweler's magnifier that is held up to the eye, and unrelated to sun glare.
Sunglasses styles.Microscope: Microscopes reveal tiny things, which has nothing to do with shade.
Sunglasses styles.Spyglass: A spyglass is a small telescope, the classic prop of pirates, and does not tint.
Sunglasses styles.Sun visor: A sun visor shades the eyes, but it is a brim and not eyewear, so it is not a style of sunglasses.

Festivals celebrated in India.Holi: The festival of colours, with coloured powder thrown in the streets, marks the arrival of spring.
Festivals celebrated in India.Navratri: It means nine nights, and it honours the goddess Durga, with dancing like garba especially in Gujarat.
Festivals celebrated in India.Dussehra: It marks the triumph of Rama over Ravana, and in many places giant effigies of the demon king are burned.
Festivals celebrated in India.Onam: The harvest festival of Kerala honours the legendary king Mahabali, with a huge vegetarian feast on banana leaves.
Festivals celebrated in India.Pongal: A four-day harvest festival in Tamil Nadu, named after a dish of rice boiled with milk until it overflows.
Festivals celebrated in India.Raksha Bandhan: Sisters tie a protective thread called rakhi on their brothers' wrists, and the brothers promise to look after them.
Festivals celebrated in India.Janmashtami: It celebrates the birth of Krishna at midnight, with human pyramids breaking pots of curd in Mumbai.
Festivals celebrated in India.Ganesh Chaturthi: Huge clay idols of the elephant-headed god are carried to the sea or rivers and immersed on the last day.
Festivals celebrated in India.Durga Puja: The big celebration in Bengal, with elaborate temporary pavilions built, and UNESCO listed it in 2021 as intangible heritage.
Festivals celebrated in India.Baisakhi: The spring harvest festival in Punjab also marks the founding of the Khalsa by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699.
Festivals celebrated in India.Lohri: A winter bonfire festival of Punjab, where people toss popcorn and peanuts into the fire to mark the end of the cold.
Festivals celebrated in India.Makar Sankranti: It marks the sun's move into Capricorn, and kite flying is huge for it in Gujarat.
Festivals celebrated in India.Thanksgiving: It is a North American holiday, not Indian, and Americans celebrate it on the fourth Thursday of November.
Festivals celebrated in India.Oktoberfest: It is a Bavarian beer festival in Munich which starts in September and ends in early October.
Festivals celebrated in India.Hanukkah: The Jewish festival of lights lasts eight nights, and it is not from India.
Festivals celebrated in India.Mardi Gras: This is a carnival before Lent, big in New Orleans and in Rio, and it is not an Indian festival.
Festivals celebrated in India.Songkran: It is Thailand's New Year, held in April, and is famous for its huge water fights.
Festivals celebrated in India.Obon: A Japanese summer festival honouring ancestors' spirits, with lanterns and bon dances.
Festivals celebrated in India.Day of the Dead: A Mexican celebration of loved ones who have died, with marigolds and sugar skulls.
Festivals celebrated in India.Chuseok: The Korean harvest festival, similar to Thanksgiving, when families visit ancestral graves and eat songpyeon rice cakes.
Festivals celebrated in India.Tet: The Vietnamese Lunar New Year, the country's biggest holiday, and no Indian festival.
Festivals celebrated in India.Bonfire Night: A British event on 5 November, marking the failed Gunpowder Plot of 1605, with no link to Indian festivals.
Festivals celebrated in India.Midsummer: A Nordic and European festival around the summer solstice, famous in Sweden for maypoles and flower crowns.
Festivals celebrated in India.Hogmanay: Scotland's New Year's Eve party, with the tradition of first-footing, and it is certainly not Indian.

Cities that ring in the New Year before.Buenos Aires: Argentina is three hours behind London, so it is later than London.
Cities that ring in the New Year before.Anchorage: Nine hours behind London, so it celebrates long after the British.
Cities that ring in the New Year before.Vancouver: Eight hours behind London, so it comes late in the global New Year, on the West Coast.
